title: Shear-Mode-Based Cantilever Driving Low-Frequency Piezoelectric Energy Harvester Using 0.67Pb(Mg<sub>1/3</sub>Nb<sub>2/3</sub>)O<sub>3</sub>-0.33PbTiO<sub>3</sub>
venue: IEEE Transactions on Ultrasonics, Ferroelectrics and Frequency Control

sections.heading: Shear-mode-based cantilever driving low frequency piezoelectric energy harvester using 0.67Pb(Mg1/3Nb2/3)O3-0.33PbTiO3
sections.text:
Zhou Zeng, Bo Ren, Linlin Gai, Xiangyong Zhao, Haosu Luo, and Dong Wang, Member, IEEE

Abstract—Energy harvesting from external mechanical excitation has become a hot interest area and relaxor piezoelectric single crystal $( \mathbf { 1 }  – x ) \mathbf { P b } ( \mathbf { M g } _ { 1 / 3 } \mathbf { N b } _ { 2 / 3 } ) \mathbf { O } _ { 3 } – x \mathbf { P b } \mathbf { T i O } _ { 3 }$ $( \mathbf { P } \mathbf { M } \mathbf { N } { - } x \mathbf { P } \mathbf { T }$ or PMN-PT) has attracted continuous attention due to the well-known ultrahigh shear mode electromechanical response. To exploit the low-frequency application of excellent shear mode performance of the PMN-PT single crystal, we proposed Shear-mode-based CANtilever Driving Low frequency Energy harvester (S-CANDLE). The device composed of two symmetric assembled sandwich structures and a cantilever, in which sandwich structures can be driven by cantilever. An analytical method was used to illustrate high output mechanism and a FEM model of the device was also established to optimize the generated electric energy in this device. The electrical properties of the device under different excitation frequencies and load resistances were studied systematically. The maximum voltage and power density at resonance frequency $( 4 3 . 8 \ \mathbf { H z } )$ were measured to be $\mathbf { 6 0 . 8 \ V }$ and $\mathbf { 1 0 . 8 \ m W / c m ^ { 3 } }$ under a proof mass of ${ \bf 1 3 . 5 \ g , }$ respectively. Both theory and experiment results demonstrate the considerable potential of the resonance-excited shear mode energy harvester applied to wireless sensors and low-power portable electronics.

sections.heading: I. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
ecently energy harvesting from external mechanical excitation has become a hot interest area, by which energy R It could be applied in small, wireless autonomous devices, like those used in wearable electronics and wireless sensor networks. Hereinto, piezoelectric energy harvesting has attracted considerable attentions[1-4] for the outstanding advantages of simpler structure compared to other methods such as using electromagnetic and electrostatic effects when scavenging power directly from the mechanical vibration. Traditional piezoelectric materials, such as lead zirconate titanate ceramic, Polyvinylidene Fluoride (PVDF), etc., have been used widely by researchers in energy harvesters. But their relatively low piezoelectric constants and electromechanical coupling coefficient make them no longer adequate for high-end applications[5,6]. In recent years, relaxor piezoelectric single crystal $( 1 - x ) \mathrm { P b } ( \mathbf { M g } _ { 1 / 3 } \mathbf { N b } _ { 2 / 3 } ) \mathbf { O } _ { 3 } – x \mathrm { P b } \mathbf { T i O } _ { 3 }$ (PMN- $x \mathrm { P T }$ or PMN-PT) has attracted continuous attention due to the well-known ultrahigh electromechanical response[7-9]. The piezoelectric strain constant $( d _ { 3 3 } )$ and electromechanical coupling coefficient $\left( k _ { 3 3 } \right)$ could reach as high as $2 5 0 0 \mathrm { p C / N }$ and 0.94, respectively[7]. Furthermore, recent research revealed that PMN-PT single crystals have excellent thickness shear mode performance. When the crystal is poled along the ${ < } 1 1 1 >$ direction and the drive field is applied along the ${ < } 1 \bar { 1 } 0 >$ direction, $d _ { 1 5 }$ and $k _ { 1 5 }$ can reach the high values of $5 9 8 0 \mathrm { p C / N }$ and $9 7 \%$ , respectively[10]. However, as a certain difficulty exists to exert the shear stress, applications based on the shear mode single crystal have seldom been reported.

In 2010, Ren et al. introduced an accelerometer structure to exploit the shear mode performance of the single crystal[11], but the top of the device was free, which made the stress loaded on the crystal very small. Also, the resonance frequency of the device was very high which was difficult to match the environment vibration. In 2012, Xu et al. introduced an structure named CANtilever Driving Low frequency Energy harvester (CANDLE), which consists of one cantilever beam, two cymbals and a metal frame, and not only lowered resonance frequency dramatically but also increased output power immensely compared with previous results of cymbal transducers[12].

In this work, to exploit the low-frequency application of excellent shear mode performance of the PMN-PT single crystal, we proposed a composite structure — shear- modebased CANDLE (S-CANDLE) for harvesting mechanical energy through combining CANDLE with high performance shear mode PMNT crystal. In this structure the shear performances of the crystal could be given full play, and a high output power was expected to be obtained in low frequency using cantilever-based resonance.

sections.heading: A. Structure of the Device
sections.text:
The structure schematic of S-CANDLE is shown in Figure 1(a). Two PMN-PT wafers are sandwiched by three copper blocks and bonded together. The sandwich structures are clamped by an aluminum alloy frame and a cantilever to form CANDLE structure. Two wafers are connected electrically in series. The device is driven to shake by a vibration source.

![](images/6c5984c97b78f4378137d8f17809c180e557935937c2ff1548528f85092ffedd.jpg)  
Fig. 1. The schematic diagram (a) and the SDOF model (b) of the proposed S-Candle device. The arrows in PMNT wafers indicate the poling direction; (c) The forces analysis of the middle copper block and one PMN-PT wafer.

sections.heading: B. Working Principle of the Devicee
sections.text:
The working principle of the proposed device can be stated as follows: The vibration of the base causes the cantilever to shake and press the sandwich structures together with the frame, so the shear forces between the wafers and the copper block are induced, which can make the wafers yield charges. Fig. 1(b) is the single degree of freedom (SDOF) model of piezoelectric energy harvester. $C$ and $K$ are mechanical damping coefficient and stiffness of the device, respectively; $M _ { e q }$ is the equivalent mass and $M _ { e q } = 3 3 M / 1 4 0 + m$ , where $M$ is the mass of cantilever and $m$ is the proof mass. According to SDOF theoretical model, the displacement of the proof mass relative to the base according to SDOF model can be expressed as[13]:

$$

$$

Here, $f ( \omega ) = \mu _ { n } ( \omega { / } \omega _ { n } ) ^ { 2 } \Big / \sqrt { [ ( 1 - ( \omega { / } \omega _ { n } ) ^ { 2 } ) ^ { 2 } + ( 2 \varsigma \omega { / } \omega _ { n } ) ^ { 2 } } ~ ;$ $Y$ is displacement amplitude of the base; $\omega$ and $\omega _ { n }$ are the excitation frequency and eigenfrequency of the device, respectively; $\zeta$ and $\phi$ are the mechanical damping factor and initial phase angle; $\mu _ { n }$ is the correction factor of the simplified SDOF model for the n-mode vibration of the energy harvesting device. Through Eq. (1), excitation forces generated by proof masses can be expressed as:

$$

Here, $a$ is the acceleration provided by the base and $a = Y \omega ^ { 2 } \sin ( \omega t - \phi )$ . Assuming that the total mass of the middle copper block $m _ { b }$ , and the mass of the PMN-PT wafer is $m _ { a }$ . Figure 1(c) shows the schematic diagram of the forces analysis. $F _ { 1 }$ is the force between the middle block and the wafer, $F _ { 2 }$ is the force between the side block and the wafer. We define the up direction to be positive for $F _ { 2 }$ and negative for $F _ { 1 }$ on the wafer (Fig. 1(c)). The up direction is also defined to be positive for the acceleration of the device. Then the Newton’s second law for the middle block and wafers can be expressed as:

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { 2 F _ { 1 } - T ( t ) = m _ { b } a } } \\ { { \nonumber } } \\ { { F _ { 2 } - F _ { 1 } = m _ { p } a } } \end{array}
$$

From which we can obtain the shear force on the wafer:

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle F _ { \mathrm { s } } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( F _ { \mathrm { 1 } } + F _ { \mathrm { 2 } } ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } [ T ( t ) + m _ { b } a + m _ { p } a ] } } \\ { { \displaystyle ~ = \frac { 1 } { 2 } [ f ( \omega ) M _ { e q } + m _ { b } + m _ { p } ] a } } \end{array}
$$

Since $( m _ { b } + m _ { p } )$ is very small compared to $M _ { e q }$ , the shear force $F _ { s }$ could be approximately expressed as: $F _ { s } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } f ( \omega ) M _ { e q } a \cdot f ( \omega )$ could be taken as the scaling factor of shear force.

A Finite Element Method (FEM) model of the device was developed using COMSOL software to optimize the performance of our device. In this model, a constant load (i.e., $1 \mathrm { N } )$ is forced on the top of middle copper block. The thickness, width of PMNT wafers were keep to be $1 \ \mathrm { m m }$ and $6 \ \mathrm { m m }$ , respectively. Fig. 3 shows average shear stress $\overline { { T } } _ { s }$ and electric energy $E$ in each sandwich structure change as a function of wafer height $H _ { p . }$ . Both of them decrease with rise in $H _ { p }$ , which means that higher electric energy could be obtained from smaller $H _ { p }$ . The insert graph shows shear stress distribution in the sandwich structures with different PMNT wafer height. As we can see, the distribution of shear stress become uneven with the increase of $H _ { p }$ , which will cause electric energy loss because of stress concentration and charge equalization[14]. Thus, a small $H _ { s }$ is expected when designing the device. However, previous researches shows that the piezoelectric coefficient $d _ { 1 5 }$ and $g _ { 1 5 }$ will decrease with reduction in $H _ { p } [ 1 0 , 1 5 ]$ . So $H _ { p }$ should be set in a moderate value in order to obtain high output electric energy.

sections.heading: IV. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
The experimental results obtained from the characterization of S-CANDLE for energy harvesting purposes are presented and discussed. Fig. 5 presents the experimental results of open circuit voltage $( U _ { o p e n } )$ and electric power $( P )$ generated in S-Candle as a function of wafer height $( H _ { p } )$ when the device were driven by shaker at the resonance frequency $( 8 7 . 3 ~ \mathrm { H z } )$ with a tip mass of $3 . 7 ~ g$ . The generated power is calculated by the formula[12]: , where $C _ { O }$ and $f$ are the static capacitance of the device and vibration frequency of mechanical excitation. As we can see, $U _ { o p e n }$ decreases with increase of $H _ { p }$ , while $P$ has a maximum value of $2 6 . 7 \mathrm { m W }$ when $H _ { p } { = } 3 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ . Such change tendency is in good agreement with the results of FEM in Fig. 3. So next experiments were carried out using the device with wafer height of $3 \mathrm { m m }$ .

![](images/8bfd862a54ada9acb8777953da6b33891e5564343d27deb8527d4f452541b0ea.jpg)  
Fig. 5. The experimental results of open circuit voltage and electric power generated in S-Candle as a function of wafer height when the device were driven by shaker at the resonance frequency $( 8 7 . 3 \mathrm { H z } )$ with a tip mass of $3 . 7 ~ \mathrm { g }$

Fig. 6 presents the frequency response functions (FRFs) of open-circuit voltage $( V _ { o p e n } )$ of the device with various proof masses. The open-circuit voltage and generated power are normalized divided by the acceleration and the square of the acceleration according to the SDOF piezoelectric energy harvesting theoretical model[12,16]. Fig. 6 demonstrates that increasing of the proof mass not only enables the device to convert more electrical energy from vibration sources but also lowers the resonance frequency of the device.

Fig. 7 illustrates equivalent mass dependence of mechanical damping factor for the device at resonance frequency. The mechanical damping factor was calculated using the formula[17]: $\varsigma = 1 / ( 2 Q ) = \Delta f / ( 2 f _ { 0 } )$ , where $\boldsymbol { Q }$ is the mechanical quality factor; $\Delta f$ is the half power bandwidth and $f _ { 0 }$ is the resonance frequency, as shown in Fig. 6. As we can see, $\zeta$ decreases with the increase of $M _ { e q }$ . This phenomenon can be explained as follows: According to SDOF model, $\zeta$ is determined by the formula[18]: $\varsigma = c \Big / \sqrt { 4 k M _ { e q } }$ , where $c$ is the damping coefficient, and a larger proof mass means a lower $\zeta .$ The mechanical damping factors in different proof masses are less than $0 . 5 \%$ , which means the scaling factor are larger than 100.

The load resistances dependence of output voltage and power of the proposed device with different proof masses are studied, as shown in Fig.8. The experiments are conducted at resonance frequency. Maximum voltage and power of the device increase dramatically with the proof mass. This property is similar to the cantilever energy harvester. Besides, matching load resistances for maximum output power also increase with the proof mass as shown in Fig. 8(b). Because larger proof mass indicates lower resonance frequency of the device, and matching load resistance can be approximately expressed by $Z = 1 / \omega C$ . Experimental results shows that a maximum output power of $0 . 7 8 ~ \mathrm { m W }$ (from two sandwiches structures, i.e., 0.38 $\mathrm { m W }$ and $0 . 4 0 \mathrm { m W } _ { : }$ , respectively) and peak voltage of $6 0 . 8 \mathrm { V }$ are obtained for the device with a proof mass of $1 3 . 5 \ \mathrm { g }$ . The power density of our device reaches as high as $1 0 . 8 ~ \mathrm { \ m W / c m ^ { 3 } }$ calculated from the formula $P _ { 0 } = P _ { o u t } / V$ , where $P _ { o u t }$ is the output electric power and $V$ is the volume of PMNT wafers [12]. The maximum output voltage and generated power density is almost 5.4 and 2.4 times as large as previous reported results of the sandwich-based energy harvester[11] $( 6 0 . 8 \mathrm { V }$ to 11.3 V, 10.8 $\mathrm { m W } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$ to $4 . 5 \mathrm { m W } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$ ), while the excitation acceleration and mass are only 1/30 and $1 / 1 5$ ( $\mathrm { 4 } \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ to $1 2 1 . 6 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ , $1 3 . 5 \ \mathrm { g }$ to 200 g) of that, respectively. Those results are coincident with the value of force scaling factor (i.e., 100) described in Fig. 7. The high output properties indicate that the S-Candle have the potential to be applied to low-power portable electronics and wireless sensors.

The experimental and theoretical maximum electric output power of the proposed device in various equivalent masses under different pre-pressure. $C { = } 0$ represents the condition where sandwich structures exactly touch the cantilever, $C { = } 0 . 5$ and $C { = } 1$ represent the conditions where screws in the device tightened by half circle and one circle compared to $C { = } 0$ , respectively.

Figure 9 shows the experiment and theory maximum electric power in various equivalent masses under different prepressure. The line with triangle symbol represents the output power without pre-pressure applied on the sandwich structures, which means the sandwiches structure exactly touch the cantilever $\scriptstyle ( C = 0 )$ . Meanwhile, the lines with tangle and circle symbol represent that with the screws tightened by half circle $( C { = } 0 . 5 )$ and one circle $\scriptstyle ( = 1 )$ ) compared to $\cdot C { = } 0 ^ { \circ }$ respectively. Two conclusions could be summarized : First, maximum electric power generated from the device presents increase trend with rise in proof mass, which means that high output results from larger shear force. Such change tendency is similar to the theoretical results calculated by Equation (10). Second, it’s the pre-pressure applied on the sandwich structures by screws when assembled that makes the experimental value higher. Because larger pre-pressure induces larger shear stress in PMNT wafers, and large shear stress means larger output power.

sections.heading: V. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
In summary, a shear-mode-based cantilever driving low frequency piezoelectric energy harvester using high performance PMNT (S-Candle) has been designed and fabricated. The device combines CANDLE with high performance shear mode PMNT crystal, in which sandwich structures can be driven by cantilever. Through resonance of cantilever, high shear stress could be induced in PMNT wafers. An analytical method used to illustrate the performance of S-ANDLE shows that the resonance-based force scaling effect is the main reason for high output properties. An FEM model was also established to optimize the generated electric energy. The electrical properties of the proposed device under different frequencies and load resistances were studied systematically. The experimental results shows that under the proof mass of $_ { 1 3 . 5 \mathrm { ~ g ~ } }$ and excitation acceleration of $1 \ \mathrm { \bf ~ g } ,$ , the device can generate an open circuit voltage of $6 0 . 8 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ and a maximum

IEEE Transactions on Ultrasonics, Ferroelectrics, and Frequency Control power density of $1 0 . 8 ~ \mathrm { \ m W } / \mathrm { c m } 3$ at $4 3 . 8 ~ \mathrm { { H z } }$ . The output properties are at least 2 times larger than that of previous reported sandwich-based energy harvester, while the input parameters are one magnitude smaller. Both theory and experiment results demonstrate the considerable potential of the device in energy harvesting applied to wireless sensors and lowpower portable electronics in low excitation frequency environment.

Haosu Luo received his B.S. degree from Nanjing Normal University, Nanjing, China, in 1982 and his Ph.D. degree from Shanghai Institute of Ceramics, Chinese Academy of Sciences (SICCAS), Shanghai, China, in 1992. He became as a professor in SICCAS in 1997. His research interests include the growth, characterization, and practical applications of ferroelectric single crystals. Current researches involve the growth of high-Tc relaxor-based single crystals, lead free piezoelectric single crystals, and device applications of these single crystals in ultrasonic transducers, high strain actuators, infrared detectors, ultrasonic motors, and various sensors. He is involved in more than 400 publications.

Dong Wang received his B.S. degree from Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China, in 1992 and his Ph.D. degree also from Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China, in 1999. From 1999 to 2004, he was a Postdoctoral in the Shanghai Institute of Ceramics, Chinese Academy of Sciences (SICCAS). He became as a professor in SICCAS in 2008. His research interests include the preparation and mechanism of high efficient lightemitting materials, the preparation of novel ferroelectric and piezoelectric materials and device design based on new inorganic functional ceramic materials as well as relaxed-based ferroelectric single crystals. He is involved in more than 50 publications.
